🗒️What This Means For You
  • Fed Hike: Since the 2026-09-16 Fed hike the Treasury-rate leg of IG returns is -1.25% (7-year +18bp). At trading day 17 (last close) it was -1.25% against a five-campaign average of -1.08% at the same point — 1994-95, 2022-23 were worse. The spread leg adds -0.28%. The 10-year is +22bp since the hike vs a +13bp campaign average at the same point. The 2s10s steepening may be topping (3 of 4 signals: topping likely).
  • HY Contagion: Junk-bond stress: the CCC-to-single-B spread gap is 719bp against a five-year average of 410bp (widest since Apr 2020). Better-rated junk is following: single-B +38bp and BB +35bp in a month. CCC and single-B are moving together more (correlation 0.21 → 0.52 over 3 months; five-year norm 0.70). Investment grade is untouched (+2bp).
  • Stocks: Stock futures are slightly higher Sunday night after a solid Friday rally.
  • FX: The dollar is slightly weaker; the euro and pound are a touch firmer.
  • Technicals: US stocks are stretched well above their averages; 10-year yields are unusually high.
  • Sectors: Safer sectors led last week; tech still leads the past month.
  • Credit/Spreads: Most corporate debt is calm, but the weakest junk bonds are under real strain.
  • Crisis: Overall stress is moderate, led by high government borrowing costs and Hormuz.
  • Inflation: Core inflation is cooling, but energy and a large group of prices stay hot.
  • Tech Bubble: Credit and volatility look like 2000 complacency; valuations are far less extreme.
  • Earnings & IPOs: JPMorgan and Interactive Brokers headline earnings; two small biotech IPOs are scheduled.
  • Iran: Peace talks are stalled and attacks near the Strait of Hormuz are increasing.
  • Warsh: The Fed chair leans toward holding or hiking rates while inflation stays sticky.
  • Week Ahead: Wednesday's inflation report and the big bank results set the week's tone.
  • Outlook: Neutral near term; stretched stocks and junk-bond strain argue for caution.
  • Trades: Trim the weakest junk bonds, buy stock dips, and keep an energy hedge.
  • Trades Vol: 45 watchlist names screened: 1 buy, 22 hold long, 22 stay out
  • Pre-market: Twelve gappers, zero catalysts in the packet, zero names on either watchlist. Nothing to trade off this sheet, so the best move is to sip the coffee and wait for Monday's actual premarket.
  • Treasury Liquidity: Treasury liquidity/rates-vol monitor: TLT 95/100 put skew +0.82 vol pts, Fed DKW real term premium +91bp.
  • 10Y Pattern: 10Y at 97th pctile, +6bp from the 2026 rim — still compressing, not a cup-and-handle.
  • Diesel Futures: Diesel: 1-9 of 10 signals point lower.
  • Bottom line: Calm on the surface; watch whether the junk-bond strain spreads upward.

Sunday-night futures are building on Friday's broad rally. ES is +0.21% (7876.5), NQ +0.34% and Dow futures +0.24%. On Friday the S&P 500 closed +0.59% at 7811.54, the Dow +0.83% and the Russell 2000 +0.46%, and VIX fell 3.70% to 14.84. Europe was stronger still (FTSE 100 +1.06%, STOXX 600 +0.97%). Sentiment is complacent but not euphoric. The S&P is 7.74% above its 200-day average with a 100th-percentile stretch reading (computed). The US 10Y at 5.2378% is also at a 100th-percentile extreme (computed). The biggest story under the surface is junk credit. The headline HY spread is a calm 3.08% (18th percentile, computed), but Bloomberg's Caa-B gap is 719bp. That is 204bp wider in three months, at the 100th percentile of its 5-year range, nearly double its 409.6bp 5-year average, and the widest since 2020-04-24 (data as of 2026-10-08). Is the CCC rot spreading? Partly. Single-B (+38bp) and Ba (+35bp) both widened over the past month, but both tightened last week (-15bp and -6bp). The B-Ba gap is only at the 31st percentile of its 5-year range, and IG is just +2bp over the month. The 63-day Caa/B correlation of daily changes jumped to 0.52 from 0.28 a month ago, so the moves are coupling more tightly. It is still below its 0.70 5-year median. This is descriptive, not a validated signal. For now the stress is concentrated at the bottom of the ladder. On geopolitics, Iran talks are stalled and attacks around Hormuz have intensified (Al Jazeera, Oct 11), yet Brent is off 1.27% tonight at 103.39. This week brings Wednesday's CPI, the money-center banks and UnitedHealth.

Two-sided analog episodes per signal: days where the signal's percentile-rank (vs its own full history) was <=5th or >=95th, or |z-score|>=1.3, clustered into one episode per zone per >=6-month gap between episode starts. For each zone, the realized forward 6-month % change in the BENCHMARK'S OUTRIGHT PRICE from each episode start is measured; a card's direction (BUY/SELL) is whichever sign that median historical move carries. Entry/target/stretch/stop are computed directly from this table -- the narrative prose (thesis/rationale) is the only part supplied by an LLM, and it is not permitted to alter a number. Crack spreads and curve shapes are, financially, relative-value signals rather than clean predictors of outright price; expressing every card in outright price terms is a deliberate simplification. HO36 Comdty (ULSD's 36-month point) is thin/less liquid on this seat -- treat its curve-shape reading with lower confidence than the others. Not investment advice.

Churn = the longest window of 20-120 sessions whose close range is <= 8x its median ATR(14), with median ADX(14) < 20, an insignificant close-price slope (p > 0.05), and >= 2 entries into each edge zone (top/bottom 20% of the band). Support/resistance = median swing low/high (+/-5 sessions); outer edges = the window's extreme closes. Breakout = a close beyond the outer edge by > 0.5 ATR, confirmed by a second close or one close beyond 1 ATR. A break back inside within 5 sessions is a failed break. An episode's outer edges can widen at most 0.5 ATR past their first detection, so a slow grind can't drag the range along with it. Base rates come from replaying the same rules over the full history, day by day, with no lookahead. This is pattern analysis of historical prices, not investment advice.

🔄Sector Analysis

Over the past week, US leadership was defensive and real-asset: Cons Staples +3.98%, Utilities +3.94%, Energy +3.62%, with Cons Discr (+3.12%) and Health Care (+2.84%) also strong. Info Tech (-0.26%) and Industrials (-0.42%) lagged. Over one month the picture flips. Info Tech leads at +6.59% with Comm Services +3.79% and Health Care +3.37%, while Financials (-3.56%), Real Estate (-2.91%) and Utilities (-2.07%) lag. Year-to-date the market is barbelled: Energy +42.47% and Info Tech +29.79%, against Utilities -4.20%, Cons Discr -1.05% and Financials -0.34%. Global sectors show the same shape: global Info Tech is +36.97% YTD and Energy +36.92%. Global Financials are -5.07% over one month and global Materials -4.57%. Interpretation: growth still leads on the one-month view, but last week's defensive bid plus weak financials suggests investors are hedging. The bid went to staples, utilities and health care, while banks were sold. Financials' one-month underperformance sets a low bar into this week's bank earnings. Energy's YTD dominance reflects the Iran/Hormuz oil premium (Brent above $100).

Near an all-time high a 63d widening past the trigger has historically raised P(SPX -10% within 3m) from ~8.6% to ~21.9% (Baa p=0.013, HY p=0.028, IG p=0.047, 1990-2026, corroborated on three independently-sourced series). 💧Treasury liquidity & rates volcomputed

US Govt Securities Liquidity Index (GVLQUSD), MOVE, Fed DKW term premium and TLT option skew, live from Bloomberg + federalreserve.gov.

Five charts tracking the mechanism Simon White laid out for why Treasury liquidity is deteriorating: rising inflation volatility feeds into a higher term premium, which steepens the curve, which raises bond vol, which shows up as worse UST market liquidity. Right now UST liquidity is at the 48th percentile of its own history (higher = worse) and the Fed's own DKW real term premium is +91bp.

Latest reading is +0.82 vol points (44th percentile of the 39 runs recorded so far). Positive means the 5%-OTM put is pricier than the at-the-money option -- the market paying up for downside-price / higher-yield insurance on long-end Treasuries.

UST liquidity index is 1.51 (48th percentile of its own 2007-present history -- 100th = worst liquidity on record), deteriorating over the past 3 months (+0.05 pts). CPI YoY volatility (2yr) is 0.49pp; the article's thesis is that rising inflation vol drags liquidity worse, which this chart is built to let you check month to month.

Real term premium is +91bp (96th percentile of its own 2007-present history), up 12bp over the trailing ~2 months. Inflation risk premium is +14bp. Fed staff's own DKW decomposition (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei) splits the rise in long yields into a policy-uncertainty component (real term premium) and an inflation-uncertainty component -- both rising is the article's read that this move isn't just a rate-expectations story.

MOVE is 98.5 (71th percentile of its own post-2007 history). The 3m10s curve is 108bp (steeper by 31bp over 3 months). The article's claim is mechanical, not just correlated -- a steeper curve gives forward rates more room to move before converging to spot, which is itself higher realized/implied vol.

MOVE and the UST liquidity index have moved together with a full-history correlation of +0.72 (both series read as 'worse' when they rise). That's the closing link in the article's chain: inflation vol -> term premium -> curve steepness -> bond vol -> liquidity.

Recreates 5 charts from Bloomberg MacroScope, 'Treasury Market Liquidity Is a Live Issue Again' (Simon White, 19-Aug-2026). TLT skew accumulates one point per report run -- Bloomberg's option-surface field is snapshot-only, not retrievable historically via the API. Term premium is the Fed's own DKW model series (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei), pulled directly from federalreserve.gov, not Bloomberg. Not a trading signal -- a liquidity/vol monitor only.

Retracement of the left-rim decline: 76% (needs ≥90% to pass). 10Y level that passes: 6.16% (92bp above today).
Retracement = (right rim − cup base) / (left rim − cup base) = (5.30 − 0.51) / (6.79 − 0.51) = 76%.
Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base) = 0.51 + 0.90 × (6.79 − 0.51) = 6.16%.

Same test on each trailing window: cup base = lowest close in the window, left rim = highest close before it, right rim = highest close after it. Cup complete at ≥90% retracement; above 110% the yield has run past the old high (a breakout, not a cup). No cup inside the window when its left rim is not the highest close of the 91 days before it, i.e. yields were already falling into the window. Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base).

🗞️Street View — Where the Cycle Is HeadingCURATED · AS OF 2026-10-01

⚠ Commentary is 10 days old (as of 2026-10-01); it may not reflect the latest Fed news.

Consensus is a short, shallow campaign: one or two more 25bp hikes, December more likely than October. The debate is whether hiking into an energy shock ends in recession, and the bond market is already doing some of the tightening.

The Fed

  • Sept 16: unanimous 25bp hike to 3.75–4.00%, the first since 2023. Dots: median one more hike in 2026; 16 of 18 see at least one, 4 see two. Inflation not back at 2% until 2029. (CNBC, FedAndMarkets)
  • Warsh's message was distinctly hawkish (inflation 'too high and broad-based'); the Conference Board calls it 'not a one and done'. (Conference Board)
  • Sept 29, Williams (NY Fed): 'no need for urgency'; one more hike 'late this year' may be appropriate; the biggest inflation shocks have passed. (Bloomberg, NY Fed)
  • Sept 30, August PCE came in soft: headline 3.4% (vs 3.7% expected), core 3.0% (vs 3.3%). October odds fell; December still priced. Kashkari: inflation 'still too high'. (CNBC, CNBC (Kashkari))

Market pricing

  • October 28 hike odds vary widely by venue, roughly 35% to 69% (prediction markets highest, CME futures ~58%), mostly measured before the soft PCE print. (PredictionMarketsPicks)
  • About 83% odds of another hike by year-end; futures price ~93bp of tightening over the next 9 meetings, more than the dots. (Forbes)

Bonds and credit

  • 10-year Treasury above 5.25% (Sept 28), the highest since 2007; 30-year ~5.49%. Drivers cited: sticky energy inflation (Iran war), heavy issuance, AI capex demand. Term premium ~1.0–1.4%. (CNBC, CNBC (Warsh's yield problem))
  • AI-related issuers trade ~115bp vs ~78bp for IG overall; high-yield AI supply $40B year to date vs $12B in all of 2025. BNP and Goldman warn the issuance could pressure spreads. (Reuters, Bloomberg (BNP))

The bear case

  • Rosenberg: the Fed has never hiked into an energy shock without a recession, and AI won't save it this time. (TheStreet)
  • Goldman called the case for hiking 'weak' (demand not overheating, energy inflation should fade when the war ends). Oxford Economics: 'The Fed cannot control energy prices'; the risk is a weaker labor market. (CNN)

Read-through: For bonds, the bigger risk is the long end, not the Fed: term premium and supply keeping the 10-year above 5% matter more than one extra 25bp. The recession call is loud but isn't in any sell-side house view yet.

Curated summary of published Fed, market and economist commentary (news and research via the web), not a computed series and not a forecast. Odds differ by venue and move daily.

🔥Is Inflation Persistent?

Persistence score: 56/100 — Inflation is moderately persistent. Underlying trend measures are drifting lower, but headline and energy-driven prices keep a meaningful share of the basket hot. Every trimmed and median measure is reported as falling: Median CPI 2.58%, 16% Trimmed-Mean CPI 2.57%, Median PCE 2.57%, Trimmed-Mean PCE 2.19%, Core Sticky CPI 2.70%. Their z-scores sit near zero, so core trend is roughly at its historical norm, not running away. Core PCE at 3.00759% YoY still exceeds the trimmed measures. That suggests a few large components are pushing the average up. Breadth is the concern. The Dallas distribution shows 13.2% of the PCE basket rising above 10% and 15.7% rising 5-10%, so nearly 29% is running at 5%+. Flexible CPI is 4.94% (76th percentile, z 0.54), which fits oil above $90. The offset is that 25.8% of the basket is outright falling. Short-run expectations (1y breakeven 2.8074%) sit above longer-run (5y 2.3709%). The market sees an energy-led hump, not an entrenched spiral. Wednesday's CPI is the test.

Bubble-analog — today's Nasdaq vs the dot-com cycle (two anchors)

WHY TWO START DATES?
Each line is rebased to 100 at a low the tech bull launched from, so elapsed time lines up. Oct-2022 is today's anchor — it was the prior bear-market bottom. Oct-1990 is the dot-com cycle's equivalent (its literal prior bear bottom). But 1990 predates the internet mania by ~4 years, so the second chart re-anchors the dot-com line to the 1994 reset low, just before the surge ignited, for a tighter like-for-like. Today sits very early under the strict 1990 analog, further along under the 1994 surge analog.
━ Anchored at the prior bear-market bottom (Oct-1990)   ━ today's cycle
━ Anchored at the pre-internet reset low (1994)   ━ today's cycle

Valuation marker: today's Nasdaq P/E (43x) ≈ 25% of the ~175x 2000-peak P/E.

IF THIS RHYMES WITH 2000
Nasdaq fell -78.0% peak→trough (2000-03-10 → 2002-10-09, ~31 months); it took ~15 years to reclaim the high.

This does not look like a dot-com top in valuation terms; it looks like a credit-complacency top in the making. Equity multiples are high but nowhere near 2000's extremes. The 2000 tell, a manic IPO market and P/Es above 100x, is absent: this week's IPO calendar is two biotech deals of $150-175M. What does rhyme with 2000 is the plumbing. Spreads are priced for perfection, volatility is low, financial conditions are loose and 10-year yields sit above 5%. In 2000, tight credit plus rising rates turned into a 78% Nasdaq drawdown over 31 months once earnings growth disappointed. My analyst estimates suggest concentration and CAPE are near or above 2000 levels. These are recalled approximations: concentration about 40%, CAPE about 40x, market cap/GDP about 220%, long-term EPS-growth expectations about 70 on a 0-100 scale. That is the larger long-run risk, but the trigger signposts are not in place yet: no PMI rollover and no bank-lending tightening (SLOOS 0.0). The CCC widening is the first catalyst-type crack worth tracking.

⚔️Iran War

The war, which began Feb 28, 2026 when the US and Israel attacked Iran (Wikipedia), is in a tense diplomatic stall with intensifying maritime clashes. Al Jazeera (Oct 11) reports that attacks around the Strait of Hormuz have intensified, efforts to end the war have stalled, and no breakthrough is expected before the Nov 3 US midterms. The IRGC says a supertanker struck a mine on an unauthorised route, and US CENTCOM says it disabled a vessel trying to run the naval blockade. CNBC (Oct 8) reports that Trump said he does not want an Iran deal and that the US is reportedly preparing for 'massive bombing'. Per NBC reporting cited there, his team discussed resuming large-scale operations, with his approval at a record low amid high fuel prices. GlobalSecurity's Day-223 update (Oct 8) notes Iran has not fired directly at host states for about four weeks, though officials have threatened preemptive strikes. Houthi attacks on Saudi targets including Riyadh continue, and President Pezeshkian called negotiations 'meaningless' on Oct 6. Market read (analyst): Brent at 103.39 already prices a large premium, and tonight's 1.27% dip shows some fatigue. A renewed US bombing campaign is the main upside oil risk into the midterms. Israel's Oct 27 election is a further date to watch.

🏦Fed Chair Warsh
NEAR TERM

Next meeting: hold with a hawkish, data-dependent bias. A hike is a live option if Wednesday's CPI runs hot (inference). CNBC (Jul 31) argued his own words laid groundwork for a hike if inflation reports stayed hot. CNBC (Sep 25) reports markets still price additional increases if inflation stays elevated. No October 2026 Warsh remarks were found, so this rests on prior statements.

~1 YEAR

Higher-for-longer policy rates with the balance sheet shrinking gradually. Per his testimony, any balance-sheet change would be previewed well in advance and agreed across the FOMC, not imposed unilaterally (Invesco/Fortune/CNBC). Expect continued communications reform with less traditional forward guidance. Cuts are unlikely within ~1 year unless core trend falls clearly and labor weakens further (inference; payrolls only 29k).

Warsh's record is consistent: inflation credibility first, a smaller Fed footprint second, and less hand-holding of markets. At his June press conference he set up task forces on communications, the balance sheet, data, productivity/jobs and inflation frameworks (Fed transcript). He has since dropped traditional forward guidance (CNBC, Sep 25), which raises the market's sensitivity to each data print. Today's data tension: core trend measures are falling, but Core PCE is 3.00759% and flexible CPI 4.94%. The 10Y at 5.2378% means the market is already doing some tightening. Analyst inference: he is more likely to hold and let term premium work than to hike into a CCC credit squeeze, unless CPI surprises up. That reading is not stated by Warsh.
